neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Reports 'going somewhere else' during episodes — dissociation. Tearful when discussing work events.
neurological_exam.motor: Left arm weakness 3/5 on formal testing. POSITIVE Hoover sign — left hip extension returns to 5/5 with contralateral right leg flexion resistance. Arm falls slowly on arm drift test rather than promptly as in organic hemiparesis.
neurological_exam.sensory: Left hemisensory loss — stops exactly at the midline on face, truncal testing. Vibration intact throughout both sides.
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal right. Cannot test left arm formally due to apparent weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Left leg dragging. Observed to walk normally when exiting elevator with colleagues.
neurological_exam.additional: As an ICU nurse, patient has witnessed and managed functional episodes in patients before. She is ambivalent about her own diagnosis. Arm falls slowly during drift test — in organic UMN lesion, arm drops promptly with pronation.

patient.chief_complaint: Left-sided weakness and episodes of dissociation/unresponsiveness — 4 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. A is a 38-year-old ICU nurse who presents with a 4-week history of left arm and leg weakness and episodes of dissociation with partial unresponsiveness. She has been the lead nurse on several overnight resuscitations and approximately 3 months ago a young patient died during a code that she led. The hospital conducted a review process that, while concluding she acted appropriately, was stressful and prolonged. She has been experiencing intrusive memories of the resuscitation, avoidance of code situations, sleep disturbance, and survivor guilt. Her current neurological symptoms began approximately 3 weeks after the anniversary of that patient's death. The episodes of unresponsiveness have occurred 4 times: each lasting 1-3 minutes, she reports feeling like she 'leaves her body,' is aware but unable to respond, with immediate recovery and full recollection of what occurred during the episode. Her colleague witnessed one episode in the staff break room: patient was sitting, eyes half-open but unresponsive to voice, no limb movements, full recovery within 2 minutes. She has migraines with aura controlled on topiramate. She is worried her topiramate is causing cognitive side effects (word-finding difficulties, which is a known side effect). She denies that her symptoms could have a psychological basis, stating 'I know what real neurological disease looks like.'

mri.impression: Normal brain MRI without and with contrast. No restricted diffusion, no T2/FLAIR signal abnormality, no abnormal enhancement, no mass effect. No white matter lesions. Normal cortical ribbon pattern. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.morphology: NO EEG CHANGE during entire episode. Normal continuous background. Remarkably, patient REPORTED the content of nursing staff conversation correctly post-episode ('you said not to page the attending') — this demonstrates preserved awareness despite apparent unresponsiveness. No ictal pattern.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. One clinical dissociative episode was captured. The EEG showed continuous normal background activity throughout the episode with no ictal correlate, no electrodecrement, and no post-event slowing. No epileptiform discharges. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Normal MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine. No intramedullary signal abnormality, no cord compression, no demyelinating plaque, no leptomeningeal enhancement. Clinical correlation recommended.

warnings: Topiramate is associated with dose-dependent cognitive side effects including word-finding difficulties (aphasia-like symptoms) and processing speed slowing. These are common at doses above 50 mg/day but can occur at lower doses in sensitive individuals.
Current dose 50 mg/day total is at the lower end — consider dose reduction to 25 mg/day if cognitive effects are causing functional impairment

Topiramate's neurological side effect profile (word-finding difficulty, processing speed slowing) is distinct from the motor and sensory symptoms being evaluated; the drug interaction query is limited to pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions
alternatives: Alternative migraine prophylaxis: amitriptyline, propranolol, valproate — note amitriptyline/SNRI may be preferred given concurrent PTSD

results.title: Healthcare worker burnout and functional neurological disorder

output.summary: Published case series and surveys document FND presentations among healthcare workers in the context of occupational trauma and burnout. Survey data suggest that healthcare workers with medical knowledge frequently experience greater difficulty accepting psychological or neurobiological explanations for neurological symptoms compared to non-healthcare populations. Randomised trial evidence supports trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy for PTSD-related functional neurological presentations. FND-specific physiotherapy combined with psychological treatment has demonstrated benefit in cohort studies of patients with comorbid PTSD and FND.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — functional left hemimotor syndrome and dissociative PNES, with comorbid PTSD

differential.diagnosis: Complex partial seizures with postictal Todd's paralysis
differential.key_features: Video-EEG shows no EEG correlate during episode; patient has FULL MEMORY of events during episode (epileptic patients have amnesia for ictal events); no post-ictal confusion

Known migraines with aura but aura never previously motor; current episode duration (4 weeks) far exceeds migraine aura (<60 min); MRI normal with no spreading depression pattern; Hoover sign positive
Topiramate level therapeutic; topiramate causes cognitive/sensory side effects but not hemimotor deficit; Hoover sign positive confirms functional mechanism
MRI DWI negative; episodes too prolonged (2-4 minutes with full recovery and memory) for TIA pattern; positive functional signs on exam

Therapeutic topiramate; normal metabolics; prolactin not elevated

critical_actions: Video-EEG event capture — preserved memory during episode is pathognomonic of dissociative PNES
Therapeutic alliance with healthcare worker who resists psychological explanation
PTSD treatment as the underlying driver
Topiramate dose review for cognitive side effects
contraindicated_actions: Antiepileptic drug increase or change — not epilepsy
Dismissing symptoms because patient 'should know better' as a healthcare professional
key_reasoning_points: Dissociative PNES: patient retains FULL MEMORY of events during apparent unresponsiveness — this is pathognomonic of dissociative PNES; epileptic patients have amnesia for ictal events
Healthcare workers with medical knowledge often strongly resist FND diagnosis — therapeutic communication must validate the neurobiological basis of FND while being honest about diagnosis
Topiramate word-finding side effects are distinct from FND motor symptoms — topiramate level is therapeutic and dose reduction can address cognitive symptoms separately
PTSD with prominent dissociation is the primary driver — trauma-focused therapy addressing the patient death and code review is the therapeutic priority

red_herrings.data_point: History of migraines with aura on topiramate
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute left-sided weakness to hemiplegic migraine variant or topiramate toxicity
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Migraine aura is transient (<60 min) and never previously motor; topiramate level is therapeutic; sustained 4-week hemimotor deficit with positive Hoover sign is functional

metadata.notes: Straightforward FND in ICU nurse with PTSD from patient death. Dissociative PNES with preserved memory during episodes is diagnostic.
